name: Hair system / toupee
lead: A toupee is a hairpiece or partial wig of natural or synthetic hair worn to cover partial baldness or for theatrical purposes; the word comes from the French toupet, meaning a tuft of hair.[1] In modern hair-loss communities the term hair system usually refers to a custom-made, non-surgical hair prosthesis, typically fixed to the scalp with adhesive or tape, that replaces or fills in lost hair.[1] Wearers use it to have a full-looking head of hair straight away, in a chosen colour, density and style, without waiting for medication to work or paying for surgery.

Hairpieces are among the oldest hair-loss solutions. Wig-wearing is documented from the ancient world, wigs returned to European fashion in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries partly to compensate for hair loss, and the toupee as a men's product grew in the United States from the nineteenth century into a mass market by 1970.[1][7] Dermatology literature now lists hairpieces among the hair camouflage options, alongside scalp micropigmentation, for people whose hair loss cannot be fully treated medically or surgically.[3]

Published research on hair systems is small. A 2024 case series from Madrid of six patients examined hair loss linked to hair systems and asked whether it arises from traction or from pressure.[4] A 2025 UK survey of dermatology clinicians looked at how easily NHS-funded wigs can be prescribed for medical hair loss.[6] No trial has compared hair systems with other treatments for appearance or quality of life.

On looksmaxxing forums, hair systems are discussed as one of several routes for men with hair loss, alongside drug treatment, transplantation and a shaved head, and as a way to change style at will.[8][9]

chain: Custom base with natural or synthetic hair is fitted to the scalp
Covers thinning or bald areas while worn
A full-looking head of hair and a choice of styles
angle.text: A hair system gives the appearance of a full head of hair immediately and can be restyled, without drugs or surgery. The effect lasts only while it is worn.

infobox: Natural or synthetic hair on a fine base, often lace or similar material[1][7]
Adhesive (usual method), elastic band, or hair weaving[1]
Regular replacement; some wearers own two or three pieces[1]
Wigs for chemotherapy and alopecia areata; NHS-funded wigs in the UK[6][7]

paras: Toupees are often custom-made, using synthetic or human hair.[1] Production ranges from individual local craftsmen to large wig manufacturers.[1] In the 1950s, Max Factor-style designs sewed individual strands to fine, flesh-coloured lace so the piece looked nearly invisible; Wikipedia says Factor supplied most Hollywood actors.[1]

Adhesive is described as the usual attachment method, an elastic band appears in cheaper versions, and hair weaving, in which the base is woven into the wearer's own hair, was popular in the 1980s and 1990s.[1] A very thin piece attached with medical adhesive and worn for weeks at a time is described as non-surgical hair replacement.[1]

Wikipedia's article on wigs describes the main materials. Synthetic fibre comes in set colours and needs no sorting by grain direction, and modacrylic fibre in the 1960s made synthetic pieces more affordable.[7] Human hair, particularly Remy hair, whose cuticles are kept intact and aligned, is valued for reduced tangling.[7] Bases are often hand-tied strand by strand into fine French or Swiss lace, with a flesh-coloured lace at the front that is hard to see when worn, while wefts sewn onto a foundation are a more basic construction.[7]

Wigs date to the ancient world: Egyptians often shaved their heads and wore wigs as sun protection, and Assyrians, Greeks and Romans also wore them.[7] Their use declined in the West after the fall of the Western Roman Empire and returned in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries for appearance, hygiene and to compensate for hair loss, spread by royal patronage; Louis XIII reportedly began wearing wigs around 1624 after balding early, and periwigs reached England with Charles II in 1660.[7] A hair-powder tax in 1795 effectively ended the fashion for wigs in Britain.[7]

The toupee developed in the eighteenth century and lost popularity after the French Revolution; its use grew in the United States in the nineteenth century, when one researcher links it to a shift in how people viewed aging and men wanted to look younger.[1] Sears sold toupees by mail order from 1900, and the first toupee patent was filed in 1921; the first patent for a hairpiece followed in 1956.[1] More than 60 toupee patents and over 260 hairpiece patents have been filed with the U.S. Patent Office since 1790.[1]

Several manufacturers began advertising in major magazines and newspapers in 1954, and more than 350,000 U.S. men were estimated to wear hairpieces in the 1950s.[1] In 1959 Time estimated U.S. toupee sales at 15 million dollars a year, and in 1970 it estimated that over 2.5 million U.S. men wore toupees out of 17 to 20 million balding men, attributing the growth to better technology, a desire to look youthful and longer hairstyles.[1]

Demand among men declined afterwards. Alternatives noted in the literature include comb-overs, minoxidil and finasteride (FDA-approved for hair loss in the 1990s), hair transplantation (which has often replaced toupees among wealthier people, especially screen celebrities), shorter haircuts fashionable since the 1990s, and shaving the head.[1] A Japanese wigmaker, Aderans, reported new orders from male customers falling 30 percent between 2002 and 2004, and manufacturing has shifted from the United States to Asia.[1]

Pattern hair loss is common: Wikipedia's article on androgenetic alopecia says it affects roughly 30 to 50 percent of men by age 50 and describes male pattern loss as a moderately stressful condition that can reduce body-image satisfaction, though most men cope and keep their sense of self.[10] Dermatologists reviewing camouflage options say hair loss can affect quality of life in ways that are hard to appreciate and that camouflage should be presented when medical and surgical treatments are insufficient.[3]

Hair systems appeal to men for whom drugs are not enough or hair transplantation is limited. The same review notes that hair transplantation is constrained when the donor area is compromised.[3] Forum posters describe a system as the middle path between treatment and going bald.[8]

Scalp micropigmentation, a cosmetic tattoo that imitates tiny hair follicles or a close buzz cut, is the more permanent camouflage option named alongside hairpieces in the 2022 dermatology review.[3][11] Wikipedia says it usually takes three to four sessions of about two hours, can hide transplant scars, and can be removed with laser, and that a poorly done hairline can look unnatural.[11]

Surgical hair transplantation moves follicles from a donor area to thinned or bald areas by strip harvesting or follicle extraction.[12] Medical treatments such as finasteride and minoxidil act on the follicle and are discussed in their own articles. The Toupee article lists the comb-over, non-surgical hair replacement, medication, transplantation and accepting baldness as the main alternatives.[1]

Advertising has often shown wearers swimming and water-skiing, but Wikipedia notes that saltwater and chlorine can quickly wear out a toupee and that some shampoos and soaps damage fibres, which cannot regrow.[1] Pieces need regular replacement because of wear, expanding bald areas and changes in the shade of the wearer's remaining hair, and some wearers own two or three so that one can be cleaned while another is worn.[1]

Wigs and hairpieces are also worn by people with hair loss from chemotherapy or alopecia areata.[7] A 2025 survey of 75 dermatology clinicians from 48 of 136 UK trusts and health boards (35 percent) found that half of responding institutions reported difficulty prescribing NHS wigs and 11 percent said it was impossible, with access easier in Scotland and South West England and hardest in Northern Ireland and London; the authors concluded the variation could not be justified.[6] The paper describes wigs as a medical orthotic for some patients with alopecia and was prompted by reports from the patient group Alopecia UK.[6]

Toupees have long been the target of jokes in Western culture, typically that the wearer does not realise the piece fails to hide baldness; an early example is George Cruikshank's 1837 illustration in The Comic Almanack of a toupee blown off by wind.[1] Wikipedia lists many actors, comedians and public figures as wearers, among them Humphrey Bogart, Frank Sinatra, John Wayne and William Shatner, and notes that John D. Rockefeller began wearing hairpieces after alopecia in 1901.[1] Today, Wikipedia says, some websites focus on suspected celebrity wearers.[1]

No studies were found testing hair systems as an appearance intervention. Related published work includes a 2022 review of hair camouflage by Daruwalla, Dhurat and Hamid in the International Journal of Trichology that places hairpieces, wigs and toupees among camouflage options up to scalp micropigmentation,[3] a 2024 letter in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology by Gil-Redondo and colleagues describing alopecia attributed to hair systems in six patients,[4] and the 2025 study of NHS wig provision.[6]

The 2024 case series reports hair loss in six wearers of hair systems and examines whether traction or pressure is responsible.[4] Wikipedia says hair weaving can cause discomfort and hair loss from repeated retightening, with permanent loss along the weave line possible after about six months, and that it is therefore usually not recommended now.[1] Wikipedia's article on traction alopecia lists extensions, weaves and hairpieces attached to braids as a substantial risk because the natural hair keeps growing and the piece must be removed and reattached often, adding tension each time; it says management involves stopping the chronic traction.[5]

Forum members describe hair systems as the middle option between treatment or transplantation and going bald.[8] One thread's author sets out three choices for men with baldness, which are drug treatment with possible transplantation, a hair system if that is not possible, and baldness. He says partners often respond positively once they learn a man wears one and that a system lets a man change styles; other members of that community treat such claims sceptically.[8]

A separate thread asks whether a system suits a man who is not balding but has thick hair that is hard to spike up; one reply says it is not worthwhile unless balding.[9] In a general hair-loss thread, posters name minoxidil and finasteride as the common advice and one describes trying scalp massage for a receding hairline while calling it possibly a cope.[13]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hair systems are presented as a concealment option for balding men and are compared with medication, transplants and baldness.[8]

claims.claim: A hair system is a better option than being bald when treatment is not possible.
claims.believers: Proponents say a wearer appears to have hair nearly all the time and can change styles, and report that some partners reacted favourably after learning of it.[8]
claims.experts: Dermatology reviews list hairpieces as a camouflage option when other treatments are limited, but no study has measured their effect on attractiveness or social perception.[3]

claims.claim: A hair system looks better than a thinning or shaved head.
claims.believers: The originator of a looksmax.org thread presents hair systems as one of three options for balding men, saying that wearers appear to have hair nearly all the time.[8]
claims.experts: No published study has measured how observers rate men wearing hair systems compared with bald or shaved men.[3]

claims.claim: A hair system can be used by men who are not balding to get a style that their own hair cannot hold.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster with thick, hard-to-style hair asks whether a system would let him get a spiked style without daily styling; a reply argues that it is not worthwhile unless balding.[9]
claims.experts: No published studies address cosmetic use of hair systems by men with full hair.

claims.claim: Attachment methods can cause hair loss.
claims.believers: Wearers who develop thinning around attachment sites describe it as a downside of fixed systems, and the 2024 case series records six such patients.[4]
claims.experts: The case series asked whether the hair loss arises from traction or from pressure, and Wikipedia says hair weaving can cause traction alopecia after repeated retightening.[1][4][5]

claims.claim: Toupees are always obvious to observers.
claims.believers: Popular culture treats the toupee as a joke, and websites speculate about celebrity wearers.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that the Max Factor lace construction of the 1950s was designed to be nearly invisible, and no study has measured how often observers detect modern systems.[1]

claims.claim: Heavy scalp massage can restore a hairline by breaking up skull calcification.
claims.believers: A poster in a hair thread says they are trying what they call detumescence therapy, describing it as heavy scalp massage, while also calling it possibly a cope.[13]
claims.experts: No published studies support this mechanism of skull calcification breaking up through massage.

claims.claim: Hair transplants have largely replaced toupees for those who can afford them.
claims.believers: Forum posts treat transplantation, with a system as the fallback, as the usual order of options.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says transplantation has often replaced toupees among wealthier people, especially on-screen celebrities, while a dermatology review notes transplantation is limited where donor hair is scarce.[1][3]

card.summary: A custom non-surgical hairpiece for balding men; it covers hair loss while worn, with no trials and documented traction hair loss in some wearers.
card.note: Adhesive and weave attachments are linked to traction-type hair loss in case reports.

quick.overview:
A hair system is a custom-made hairpiece, usually attached with adhesive or tape, that covers or fills in areas of hair loss. Toupees have been sold for more than a century and remain one option alongside drugs, transplants and shaving the head.

It is a camouflage rather than a treatment: appearance changes only while it is worn, and no trial has measured its effect.
quick.mechanism: A base of fine lace or similar material carries natural or synthetic hair and is fixed to the scalp by adhesive, elastic or by weaving it into existing hair.
quick.risks: A 2024 case series reported hair loss in six hair system wearers, and weaving methods are linked to traction alopecia. Pieces need regular replacement and care; saltwater, chlorine and some shampoos damage fibres.
